About: The Compound Microscope

Source

Topic
Geometric optics — optical instruments (Class 12, NCERT Physics Part II, Ch. 9.9)
Simulation
One optical bench: specimen, objective, the real intermediate image inside the tube, and the eyepiece used as a magnifier on it.
Sign convention
Real-is-positive (Cartesian). Light travels left to right; distances are measured from the lens; u > 0 for a real object on the left; v > 0 for a real image on the right; 1/u + 1/v = 1/f and m = −v/u.
Tube length
L is the NCERT tube length: the distance from the objective's second focus Fo′ to the eyepiece's first focus Fe. The lens separation drawn on the bench is fo + L + fe.
Serves
Thin-lens equation applied twice; linear vs angular magnification; M = mo × me; normal adjustment vs near-point adjustment; why the final image is virtual and inverted.
Inquiry
Predict — before touching the objective slider — what a LONGER objective focal length does to the magnification.
Misconception
"A longer / bigger objective always magnifies more." The two instruments that share this pair of lenses do not agree, and the sim puts both numbers on screen.

Pedagogy principles applied

IDPrincipleHow it shows up here
A1One concept, one sentence"The objective makes a real, enlarged image inside the tube; the eyepiece magnifies that image." Everything on screen serves it.

K1Fill the frameThe bench spans the canvas; the intermediate image is the tallest thing in it.
K2Scale is declared, never assumedAlong the axis the bench is TRUE to scale in millimetres. Across the axis a single uniform transverse scale is used for object and image alike, and its exaggeration factor is printed on the canvas.
K3Every named quantity is drawnfo, fe, uo, vo, L, Fo, Fo′, Fe, the object, the real intermediate image and the emerging bundle are all rendered and labelled, not merely numeric.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Two lenses in a tube

A compound microscope has two converging lenses. The specimen sits just beyond the objective's focal point, so the objective forms a real, inverted, enlarged image inside the tube. The eyepiece is then used as a magnifier on that image.

2 · A longer objective

A telescope magnifies more when its objective has a longer focal length. Keeping the eyepiece and the tube unchanged, what does a longer objective do to this microscope's magnification?

3 · Compare two objectives

Set the objective's focal length to 20 mm, then to 4 mm, leaving the eyepiece and the tube alone. Compare the real image the objective forms inside the tube in the two cases.

4 · A shorter eyepiece

The eyepiece is replaced by one of half its focal length; the objective and the tube are unchanged. What happens to the total magnification?

5 · The same pair as a telescope

An astronomical telescope built from these two lenses has magnification −fo/fe. With fo = 8 mm and fe = 25 mm, what would that telescope do?

6 · The one thing to notice

In a microscope the objective's focal length divides; in a telescope it multiplies. That is why a microscope objective is a stubby few-millimetre lens while a telescope objective is long. The image you finally look at is virtual and upside down.

Fixed: near point D = 250 mm, specimen height ho = 0.10 mm. A negative magnification means the image is upside down.

Objective — the thin-lens equation

Real-is-positive convention: uo > 0 for the real object on the left, vo > 0 for the real image formed on the far side, m = −v/u. The object sits just beyond Fo, so uo is a little larger than fo.

Eyepiece — used as a magnifier

D = 25 cm is the least distance of distinct vision. The upper line is normal adjustment (final image at infinity, eye relaxed); the lower line is near-point adjustment.

Total magnification

The total is the PRODUCT of the two, never the sum. L is the tube length measured from Fo′ to Fe, which is why the standard form is exact here in normal adjustment.

Microscope against telescope

The same fo that DIVIDES a microscope's magnification MULTIPLIES a telescope's. One pair of lenses cannot be good at both jobs.

Compound Microscope

01

At a glance

A compound microscope uses two converging lenses in turn. The objective makes an enlarged image of a tiny specimen, and the eyepiece magnifies that image for the eye.

What you'll learn

  • How the objective makes a real, inverted image inside the tube.
  • How the eyepiece, used as a magnifier, gives the final image the eye sees.
  • How the two lenses, the tube length and the eye's adjustment set the total magnification.
The apparatus. The tube length L is measured from the objective's second focus Fo′ to the eyepiece's first focus Fe.

What's on screen

  • Objective: the blue lens at the left, labelled with its fo.
  • Eyepiece: the pink lens, labelled with its fe, and the eye beyond it.
  • Image and rays: the amber arrow is the real image, and amber lines are the rays.
  • Distances: rows above the axis give vo and L, and a boxed detail zooms in near the objective.
See itUse the opening setup, fo = 8.0 mm, fe = 25 mm and L = 160 mm. Watch for: the specimen at the far left, a blue objective, a long amber image arrow pointing down, then the pink eyepiece and the eye.

03

The objective makes a real, inverted, enlarged image

The specimen sits just beyond the objective's focal point Fo, at distance uo. The thin-lens equation places its image:

1/uo + 1/vo = 1/fo    mo = −vo/uo
The minus sign in mo means the image is inverted.
  • At the opening values uo = 8.40 mm, only 0.40 mm beyond Fo = 8.0 mm. At bench scale that gap is about one pixel, so a boxed detail enlarges it.
  • The image forms at vo = 168.0 mm, with mo = −20.00. The 0.10 mm specimen gives a real image 2.00 mm tall.
  • The tube length L runs from Fo′ to Fe. At the opening values the lenses are 8 + 160 + 25 = 193 mm apart.

Because the image is real, light really converges there. A screen placed at the amber arrow would show it.

See itKeep the opening setup and read the object and image distances. Watch for: uo = 8.40 mm, vo = 168.0 mm, mo = −20.00×, and "height 2.00 mm" beside the image.
04

The eyepiece magnifies the real image for the eye

The eyepiece is a simple magnifier. Its magnification me compares the angle at the eye with the angle the same object makes at the near point, D = 250 mm (25 cm).

  • Normal adjustment. The real image sits exactly on Fe, so the rays leave the eyepiece parallel. The final image is at infinity and the eye is relaxed. me = D/fe = 250/25 = 10.00.
  • Near-point adjustment. The image sits slightly inside Fe, so the rays leave spreading. The final image is virtual, 25 cm from the eye. me = 1 + D/fe = 11.00.

The two forms differ by exactly 1. In both cases the final image is virtual and still inverted compared with the specimen. No light reaches it, but the eye focuses the rays that enter it.

See itSet Eye adjustment to Near point, keeping fe = 25 mm. Watch for: me = 11.00×, dashed lines running back behind the eyepiece, and a caption saying the final image is 250 mm to its left.
05

The total magnification is the product of the two

The eyepiece magnifies the image the objective made, so the two factors multiply. They never add:

M = mo me = −(L/fo)(D/fe)
Exact in normal adjustment, because L is measured from Fo′ to Fe.

Here is why. In normal adjustment vo = fo + L. The lens equation gives vo/uo = (vo − fo)/fo, so |mo| = L/fo.

At the opening values M = (−20.00)(10.00) = −200.0. The angle at the eye is β = 4.58°, against α = 0.023° for the specimen held at 25 cm. Their ratio is 200.

In near-point adjustment the standard form −(L/fo)(1 + D/fe) gives −220.0. The sim's exact value is −223.1, because the image shifts slightly and mo becomes −20.28.

See itReturn to the opening setup, with Eye adjustment on Normal. Watch for: mo = −20.00× and me = 10.00× in the readouts, with M = −200.0× in green below the bench.
06

A shorter objective or eyepiece gives a larger magnification

Both focal lengths sit in the denominator of M = −(L/fo)(D/fe). With L = 160 mm in normal adjustment:

fofemomeM
16 mm25 mm−10.0010.00−100.0
8 mm25 mm−20.0010.00−200.0
4 mm25 mm−40.0010.00−400.0
8 mm50 mm−20.005.00−100.0
8 mm10 mm−20.0025.00−500.0

The sim holds L, the focus-to-focus gap, so changing fo or fe moves the lenses apart. A longer L raises |M| in proportion. Across the sliders |M| runs from 30× (fo = 20 mm, fe = 50 mm, L = 120 mm) to 1250× (fo = 4 mm, fe = 10 mm, L = 200 mm).

See itSet fo to 16 mm and leave the rest. Watch for: mo = −10.00× and M = −100.0×, and an image arrow half as long as before, "height 1.00 mm".
07

The same two lenses would make a telescope that shrinks

An astronomical telescope in normal adjustment has Mtel = −fo/fe. Here the objective's fo multiplies. In the microscope it divides.

  • With fo = 8 mm and fe = 25 mm, Mtel = −8/25 = −0.32. The image is smaller than the object, so these lenses would make a poor telescope.
  • A telescope needs a long objective and a short eyepiece. For example, fo = 1000 mm and fe = 25 mm give −40.
  • A telescope has Fo′ and Fe on top of each other, so its L is zero. A microscope spreads them 120 to 200 mm apart.

That is why a microscope objective is a stubby lens of a few millimetres, and a telescope objective is long. One pair of lenses cannot do both jobs.

See itReturn to the opening setup and find the telescope readout. Watch for: As a telescope −0.32× in the readouts, and a pink line under the bench saying it would shrink.
08

Where it matters

  • Laboratory microscopes. Objectives are marked with their own magnification, such as 10× or 40×, and a common eyepiece is 10×. The total is the product, so 40× with 10× gives 400×.
  • Delicate focusing. The specimen sits only 0.40 mm beyond Fo. Moving it 0.01 mm shifts the real image about 4 mm, so focusing is delicate.
  • Comfortable viewing. Normal adjustment lets the eye look at infinity, so it can stay relaxed for a long session.
  • Limits. Raising M does not reveal finer detail forever. Diffraction sets a limit, called the resolving power.
09

Summary

In one line. The objective makes a real, enlarged image of the specimen, and the eyepiece magnifies that image for the eye.

Key points

  • mo = −vo/uo = −L/fo, and me = D/fe or 1 + D/fe.
  • M = mo me = −(L/fo)(D/fe), and a telescope has Mtel = −fo/fe.

Common mix-ups

  • "Add the two magnifications." Multiply them: 20 × 10 = 200, not 30.
  • "A longer objective magnifies more." That holds for a telescope. In a microscope fo divides.

Things to try on your own

  • With L = 160 mm, find a pair fo and fe with fo × fe = 400 mm² and read M.
  • Switch to Near point and compare the exact −223.1× with the standard form −220.0×.
